analysis.one_liner: Restores the FCC's 2010 net neutrality rules struck down in court until new rules are finalized.
analysis.headline: The Open Internet Preservation Act died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote, leaving broadband providers free of net neutrality rules for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2014, a federal court struck down the FCC's 2010 net neutrality rules, which barred internet providers from blocking websites or slowing traffic. This bill would have put those rules back in effect until the FCC finished writing replacement rules. It was introduced by Rep. Henry Waxman and 36 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Communications Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have protected internet users, small websites, startups, and streaming or content services from broadband providers blocking or throttling their traffic, and would have kept the FCC's authority to enforce those protections while new rules were written.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the FCC's 2010 open internet rules — which banned blocking and unreasonable discrimination against lawful web traffic — immediately upon enactment [S2][S3].
Keeps those rules in effect until the FCC takes final action in the proceedings the court sent back to it, closing the gap left when the D.C. Circuit vacated the rules in January 2014 [S2][S3].
Preserves the FCC's ability to adjudicate violations of the rules that occurred during the protected period even after it ends, so enforcement didn't simply lapse [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers such as cable and telephone companies would bear the cost: the restored rules restricted their ability to block, slow, or charge for prioritized treatment of internet traffic, and the industry argued such rules discouraged network investment.

drawbacks.text: It was a stopgap, not a permanent framework: the bill simply reinstated 2010 rules that a federal court had already vacated as beyond the FCC's authority, so the same legal weakness that doomed the rules would still hang over them until the FCC completed its remand proceedings [S2][S3].

Broadband providers argued the anti-blocking and no-discrimination rules constrained how they could manage and monetize their networks, and that such regulation could reduce investment in broadband infrastructure — the industry case the court had found persuasive in vacating the rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a narrow bridge, not a rewrite: it restored rules protecting internet users during a period when no net neutrality rules were in effect, at the cost of limiting broadband providers' traffic-management freedom until new FCC rules were finished. Its main design weakness was that it propped up rules a court had just struck down, which critics said invited more litigation rather than resolving the underlying legal question. On balance, the public interest in an open internet during the transition was substantial relative to the temporary, limited cost to providers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications Subcommittee from February 2014 until the Congress ended in January 2015, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: On February 3, 2014, Rep. Waxman and eight original cosponsors introduced the bill to restore the FCC's vacated 2010 open internet rules until the FCC finished new rulemaking [S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on February 7 to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology [S5].
Thirty-six House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the subcommittee and full committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers benefited: for the rest of the Congress they operated with no net neutrality rules in effect after the court vacated the 2010 rules, and Congress took no action to restore them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers, free of net neutrality rules

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Sponsor; ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the FCC's vacated 2010 open internet rules during the FCC's remand proceedings.

for.name: Reps. Anna Eshoo, Doris Matsui, Mike Doyle, Zoe Lofgren, Jan Schakowsky, Frank Pallone and others
for.what_they_did: Joined Waxman as original cosponsors of the restoration bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and Communications Subcommittee leaders
against.role: Committee chairs with authority to schedule the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Communications Subcommittee on February 7, 2014, then never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Broadband industry
against.what_they_did: Had just won the court case vacating the net neutrality rules and opposed their reinstatement, arguing the rules discouraged network investment.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 supporters (the sponsor plus 36 cosponsors) were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican-led committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Broadband providers (cable, fiber, and phone companies)
industries.note: With the 2010 rules vacated by the D.C. Circuit and Congress declining to restore them, broadband providers could block, throttle, or prioritize internet traffic without net neutrality restrictions until the FCC acted later. Consumers and websites bore the risk of slower or blocked access, and paid prioritization could raise costs for small online businesses.

industries.industry: Websites, streaming services, and online startups
industries.note: These edge providers rely on neutral treatment of their traffic by broadband networks. The bill's failure left them without the anti-blocking and anti-discrimination protections during the transition, exposing them to possible tolls or throttling by internet providers.
